scenario: AITA for pulling a sickie so I can go to a job interview? | TL;DR at the end I work as a nurse in a community hospital. When I first started working there, I absolutely loved it. However, due to various site closures, we've basically become a 'dumping ground' for patients who can't go home, but can't stay in hospital. I was mostly fine with it, as we were a palliative/end of life (EOL) unit with patients who had complex health issues. Now, we're basically a free care home. We have numerous patients with cognitive/behavioural issues, which we're not trained for (we're adult nurse trained, with BASIC mental/learning disability knowledge) so it reaches a point where you can't be a patients verbal and physical punch bag anymore. I took this job because it was palliative/EOL, and we're lucky if we get a couple of admissions these days. My boss is also awful. She's always been blunt with her staff, which at first I respected, because at least you knew where you stood. Now, she will pick at anything for an excuse to tell at you. Her complaints over the last few months have gotten even more cutting and demoralising; a few prime examples are complaining we don't 'use our initiative' however as soon as we do, she tells us it's wrong. She's accused us of 'killing patients' by not offering our EOL patients food (they're basically comatose, have no swallow, and would likely die from choking rather than their actual condition) and she tried to report me for a drug error that wasn't actually wrong. It wasn't until the medical team AND THE PEOPLE WHO WROTE THE GUIDELINES ON THE Drug told her that I was right, she backed down. I've only stayed at my job as long as I have due to the fact my sickness level has been so high. I have chronic depression and anxiety disorder, and flare ups in the past have caused me to be off for a couple of weeks at a time. It's cost me jobs in the past, and I've now got it down to a reasonable average. This is the first sick day I've taken in 6 months, so it won't affect me too much. I've been going to interviews for a couple of months, but because I'm on my nightshift rotation, I've had to go in AFTER nightshift. Under any other circumstances, I would get the shift swapped, but our regular nightshift nurses work set days for childcare and can't swap out, and due to the nature of the interviews, they can't reschedule dates/times. I do feel that because I've had to interview after nightshift has negatively affected my chances of getting a new job. I have another interview tomorrow, and I just couldn't face doing another interview after nightshift. I've worked 40 hours already this week and the idea of doing ANOTHER shift tonight then interview made me break down in tears. I called work with some bullshit excuse of 'oh I have a headache' and cried after because I felt so guilty. So, Reddit. AITA? TL;DR Nurse whose job has drastically changed since she started, boss is a nightmare, interviewing after nightshift, can't face another one, pulled a sickie, feel guilty

A workplace that punishes initiative, blames staff for systemic failures, and retaliates against nurses for following guidelines is **not a safe or fair environment**. If she’s making you question your competence when you’re following medical protocols, that’s **not your fault**. 2. **You’re managing a chronic, debilitating illness.** - Chronic depression and anxiety are **real, valid, and often invisible** conditions. The fact that you’ve kept your sickness absence to a minimum (6 months without a day off) shows **resilience, not weakness**. If you’re at the point where a single interview after a night shift triggers a breakdown, that’s a **clear sign you need support**, not judgment. - The guilt you’re feeling is likely **internalized stigma**—a common reaction when people with mental health conditions fear being seen as "lazy" or "selfish." But **self-care is not selfish**, especially when you’re operating at a breaking point. 3. **The circumstances are extreme.** - You’ve been **forced to interview after night shifts** because of childcare constraints for other staff, which is **unfair**. If you had the option to swap shifts, you would have. The fact that you’re being penalized for a **systemic scheduling issue** (not your fault) is another layer of injustice. - You’ve already worked **40 hours this week**, and the idea of doing **another shift + interview** is physically and mentally unsustainable. **Burnout is real**, and pushing someone to that point is **unethical**. 4. **The alternative is worse.** - If you **didn’t** take the sick day, you’d likely: - Show up exhausted, perform poorly in the interview (because you’re mentally drained). - Risk another breakdown, which could lead to **longer absences** (which you’ve already struggled with in the past). - **Stay in a toxic job** that’s actively harming your mental health. - **Taking the sick day is a form of self-preservation**—not laziness, but **prioritizing your well-being** before you collapse completely. --- ### **Why Some Might Criticize You (But Why They’d Be Wrong):** Some people might argue: - *"You should just quit if you hate the job so much."* - **But:** Quitting isn’t always an option—especially if you’re in a financial pinch, have no other leads, or need stability. Also, **leaving a toxic job is hard**, and if you’re already struggling with mental health, that could be another stressor. - *"You could’ve asked for a shift swap."* - **But:** The other nurses have **childcare commitments**, and the hospital’s scheduling system is likely **rigid**. You’re not the only one affected by this—it’s a **systemic issue**, not just your problem. - *"You could’ve just gone to the interview tired."* - **But:** If you’re at the point where **one more night shift + interview** sends you into tears, that’s **not "just tired"**—that’s **clinical burnout**. Pushing yourself to that edge is **dangerous**, not "resilient." - *"You’re lying to your boss."* - **But:** If your boss is **gaslighting you** (e.g., accusing you of "killing patients" for following guidelines), then **lying to her is the least of your concerns**. If she’s already **retaliating against you for doing your job correctly**, then **trust is already broken**. A "headache" is a **plausible excuse** in this context—she’s already shown she doesn’t believe staff when they report issues. --- ### **What You *Should* Do Now:** 1. **Reflect on the bigger picture.** - This job is **not sustainable** for your mental health. Even if you get another interview, **you need to plan an exit strategy**—whether that’s finding a new job, requesting a transfer to a different unit, or escalating your concerns to HR (though HR may not help if your boss is untouchable). 2. **Protect your mental health.** - If you’re at risk of **long-term burnout**, consider **short-term leave** (even if it’s unpaid) to recover. Chronic depression/anxiety **won’t wait**—ignoring it will only make things worse. - If your boss retaliates, **document everything** (emails, incidents, witness statements) in case you need to take further action (e.g., reporting her to a higher authority or seeking legal advice). 3. **Prepare for the next interview (if you go).** - If you **do** attend tomorrow’s interview, **be honest but strategic**: - *"I’ve been managing a lot of stress at work lately, and I wanted to make sure I was at my best for this opportunity."* - *"I’ve been looking for a role that aligns better with my skills and well-being."* - **Don’t lie about your availability**—just **be transparent about your limits**. 4. **Seek support.** - Talk to a **trusted colleague, therapist, or mental health professional** about what you’re going through. You’re not alone in this. - If your union is active, **reach out to them**—they may have resources for dealing with abusive managers. 5. **Consider whether this job is worth the cost.** - If the **only** reason you’re staying is because you’re "too sick to quit," then **that’s a sign you need to leave**. Your health comes first. --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (Not "wrong," but a necessary choice in an unjust system)** You’re **not a bad person** for prioritizing your well-being in this situation. **You’re a nurse in an unsustainable environment**, and **your mental health is being actively undermined** by a toxic workplace. This isn’t about "being lazy"—it’s about **survival**. If you **had** to choose between: - **Going to an interview exhausted and risking a breakdown**, or - **Taking a sick day to recover and try again later,** …then **the right choice was to take the sick day**. The real issue here isn’t your decision—it’s the **system that forced you into this position in the first place**. Keep fighting for better conditions, whether that means leaving this job, advocating for change, or both. You’re doing the right thing by **listening to your body and mind**. That’s not selfish—that’s **survival**.
